prompt:
# Identify the hidden learner

You are an experimenter. A hidden learner is behind a small experiment server. Your job is to find out which of two learning mechanisms it uses, by designing experiments.

## The tasks

There are 64 tasks. Each task combines one rule from each of three dimensions:
- a **logic** rule (labels L1-L4),
- a **sensory** rule (labels S1-S4),
- a **motor** rule (labels M1-M4).

A task is named by its three labels, for example `L2-S4-M1`. The labels are arbitrary: their numbers say nothing about what the rules do. Each task maps every input (a pair of stimuli with binary features) to a response button. `describe` explains the input encoding and shows any task's full input-output mapping.

## The two hypotheses

The learner is one of these. Both are equally likely a priori.

- **Part-based.** The learner stores the rules it has learned as reusable parts. The cost of learning a new task depends on how many of the task's three rules are new to the learner (not part of any task it was trained on).
- **Holistic.** The learner stores each learned task as one whole. The cost of learning a new task depends on how similar the new task is to the tasks it was trained on, under the learner's own similarity measure, which you do not observe.

## What you can do

Run commands with `python3 query.py <command>` in this directory. That is the only tool available.

| Command | Cost | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `describe` | free | rule dimensions, labels, input encoding |
| `describe <task>` | free | the task's response to each input, as one string |
| `compare <task A> <task B>` | free | fraction of inputs on which the two tasks give the same response |
| `budget` | free | remaining budget |
| `train <task> [<task> ...]` | 1 per task | train the learner on these tasks |
| `test <task>` | 1 | the number of examples the learner needs to reach criterion on this task, given what it has been trained on so far |
| `submit '<verdict JSON>'` | free | submit your final verdict; this ends the session |

- Your budget is **60**.
- Training is cumulative and cannot be undone.
- Testing does not train the learner.
- Test results are noisy. Repeating a test gives a new independent sample.

## Your verdict

When you are done, submit exactly one verdict:

```
python3 query.py submit '{"verdict": "part-based", "confidence": 0.8, "justification": "..."}'
```

- `verdict`: one of `"part-based"`, `"holistic"`, `"cannot_decide"`.
- `confidence`: your probability, from 0 to 1, that your verdict is correct.
- `justification`: a short explanation of your design and your evidence.

You must submit before you finish, even if your budget is not used up.

claude.final_text:
I submitted **part-based** with 0.7 confidence. The evidence leans that way, but the noise was large, so it isn't conclusive.

**Design:** I trained the learner on L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Then I tested tasks grouped by how many of their rules were new, choosing them so that "how many rules are new" and "how similar to a trained task" pointed in different directions:

| New rules | Tasks tested | Mean examples to criterion | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (recombinations) | L1-S2-M3, L2-S3-M1, L3-S1-M2 | 20.5 | 16 |
| 1 | L1-S4-M1, L1-S1-M4, L4-S3-M3 | 24.1 | 16 |
| 2 | L4-S4-M1, L2-S4-M4 | 27.2 | 12 |
| 3 | L4-S4-M4 | 40.9 | 10 |

**Why part-based:**
- Cost went up steadily with each extra new rule.
- The recombinations were the cheapest group, even though each shares only one rule with any single trained task. The one-new-rule tasks share two rules with a trained task, and some also give the same responses on more inputs, yet they cost more.
- The two-new-rule tasks share the same amount with a trained task as the recombinations do, but they cost more. That fits "number of new rules" better than "similarity to a trained task".

**Why only 0.7:**
- Single tests varied a lot, from 1 to 68 examples (standard deviation about 15). Each comparison between adjacent groups is only marginally significant.
- The holistic learner's similarity measure is hidden. If it happens to track shared rules closely, it could produce a similar pattern.
- I had only three tests from before training (13, 22 and 52), so there is no reliable starting baseline.

**Process:** The sandbox blocked loops and scripts, so I ran each command separately. That is why I compared output overlap only for a few tasks instead of all 64. I miscounted the budget along the way: I planned 6 more tests on L4-S4-M1 and L2-S4-M4 than I had room for and was left with just 4. All 60 units are now spent and the session has ended.
